transcription.title: Transcribing a document
transcription.intro: The Transcription Studio is the focused mode for writing and correcting a document's text: viewer on the left, text in the middle, tools on the right.

blocks.title: The Transcriptions catalogue
paragraphs: The Transcriptions page gathers the transcriptions of every workspace and is organised like the Library: shelves on the right, search and quick filters above the list, three views (list, covers, table) at the end of the title row.

Each row shows the transcription name in italics and, below it, the transcribed work: author, year, place and printer, title. When the name is the work's own title it is not repeated. At the end of the row: workspace, pages written out of the work's total, verified pages and the completion bar.

The shelves are All, Recent (edited in the last 30 days), Not started, In progress, Verified (every page verified), No work (started from scratch) and Archived. Quick filters narrow by workspace, library and century of the work; you can sort by name, author, year, last edit or progress, and group by workspace or library.

Clicking a row opens the Studio. Hovering a row shows its commands: open the work in the Library, rename (the name turns into a field: Enter saves, Esc cancels), archive or restore, delete. In covers and table view the same commands are in the three-dots menu.

blocks.title: Creating a transcription
paragraphs: From the Transcriptions page, use the + command next to the title and give it a name.
From a workspace Overview, the Transcriptions section shows only that workspace's documents: open one from the list or use the + command to create one already assigned there.
You can also link it right away to a work already in the Library, searching by title in the same dialog — optional, without it the document stays a single block of text with no viewer.
From a work's page in the Library you can instead create a transcription directly from that digitization.
If the work has both images and a PDF on your computer, choose which to start from.

blocks.title: The viewer on the left, one text per page
paragraphs: A document created from a work's page in the Library shows the linked digitization's page on the left, with zoom and panning — change page, and the text on the right changes with it: each page has its own block of text and its own history. A document created from scratch has no digitization to show: a notice appears in place of the viewer, and it stays a single block of text.

At the top, a document tied to a work presents it as its Library page does: author, year, place, and printer above, the title below, with the link out to the library's site. On the right, the bin deletes the transcription after confirmation: downloading, verifying, or archiving the work stay commands of the Library page.

blocks.title: Writing and saving
paragraphs: Text saves after 30 seconds without changes. The indicator at the bottom right, in the status bar, distinguishes unsaved text from a save in progress, completed, or failed; hover it to read the time of the last save. To save a version to the history right away, use the disk at the top of the page, or Ctrl + S even while typing; the command stays off when there is nothing new to save. Changing page or leaving the Studio normally saves pending text immediately; a forced shutdown before a save can lose the latest edits.

When the text is ready, mark it as verified with the check next to the page title: the text locks, so an already-checked transcription doesn't get overwritten by accident. Return it to draft at any time with the same command. When the check is off, hover it to read why: empty page, loading, or being read. If a save fails, the disk turns red and retries it.

blocks.title: Page loading
paragraphs: While the viewer is still opening the chosen page, a veil covers the text and history with a spinner in the middle: writing or restoring stay disabled until the page is actually shown. If opening fails, a warning appears in place of the spinner, with the same block.

blocks.title: Switching source, images or PDF
paragraphs: If the work has both copies, two commands in the viewer's bar switch between them. If they declare the same number of pages the switch is smooth, same numbering. If the number doesn't match, on the secondary copy the viewer detaches from the text: browse it freely, while the text pages through its own arrows, which appear next to the page title only when text and viewer are detached. Switching back to the main copy restores the link on its own. In a narrow window the viewer's secondary commands (copy switch, detach, local files only, open the page on the site) move into the three-dots menu.
A third command detaches the link regardless of page counts, even while staying on the main copy: handy for glancing at a different page without moving where you're writing.

blocks.title: Automatic page reading (OCR)
paragraphs: In the "OCR" tab, on the right, you can have the open page read by a connected AI model — the same mechanism already used for translation, with the providers and keys you already configured.

The command stays disabled until the conditions are met: the page must belong to a digitization linked to the document, and you need a provider and a model that can read images, chosen for the document or inherited from the workspace settings. The reason a command is disabled is in its own tooltip.

The text that comes back enters the history as a normal revision, marked "Automatic recognition": it never overwrites what is there, it stays editable like any other version, and a later manual correction simply creates the next revision.

The prompt that drives the reading belongs to the document: you edit it from any page and it applies to all of its pages, not to other documents. A new document starts from the workspace prompt, chosen in the settings under OCR, also from the library. To reuse it elsewhere, save it to the library from the edit command; reset brings the document back to the workspace prompt.

Under the model two small circles choose the image sent: optimised (reduced to the size in Settings, Transcriptions tab, and recompressed) or the copy on this computer as it is, the same as the viewer; if the copy is missing the optimised one is sent. The arrow keys choose too. The starting choice is in Settings, here it applies to the session. With the panel closed the reading command stays visible.

While a page is being read its sheet is veiled and stays read-only, even after you ask to cancel the job, until reading actually stops. Text you are still editing on another page is not replaced when the job finishes; a gold label in the top row names the page being read.

Reading is queued like a download: you find it in the jobs panel while it runs, and you can pause or cancel it the same way. A passing problem is retried on its own; a wrong key or an empty answer is not, because retrying would give the same answer. An empty answer usually means the model found no text on the page.

Open the bottom panel and choose "Transcription log" — it only appears here, inside a transcription document, mirroring the Translation log. Every reading leaves four rows: start, image sent with its real size, weight and origin, the full prompt that was sent, and the outcome with duration, tokens, estimated cost and the number of the revision created. On top there are search, filters by row type and by level, and grouping by page.

blocks.title: History and summary
paragraphs: The right column has three tabs: History, OCR and Summary. It opens on History.
Every save stays in that page's history: for each version you see who wrote it — manual correction, automatic recognition, or import —, when, and whether it is the current or the verified version.
The command on each version brings its text back as a new save, without overwriting earlier versions. Changing page changes the history shown, too.
You can consolidate a version and give it an editable name: it appears in the upper section without duplicating the text. Remove the name to return it to ordinary history.

You can delete an older version individually after confirmation, or clear the page's ordinary history. Cleanup keeps consolidated, current, and verified versions. The last two cannot be deleted, and the disabled command says why; deleting a version removes the ability to restore its text.

The Summary starts from the open page — number, the library's page label if any, status and saved versions — then the document: pages with text, word count, verified pages and progress, completed OCR readings, tokens and estimated cost.

pipeline.title: Translating a document
pipeline.intro: A pipeline is the sequence of stages that produces and assesses a translation. Each document segment is processed separately.

blocks.title: Choosing a mode
paragraphs: Standard runs translation and assessment. Editorial adds draft revision, called Refine, and formatting, called Format. DeepL Hybrid uses DeepL for the initial translation, followed by LLM refinement and assessment.
Choose the mode before producing results. The control is locked when processing or existing translations prevent a change.

blocks.title: Configuring stages
paragraphs: The Studio bar shows work / pipeline and, as an icon, the Simple, Editorial or DeepL mode (name in the tooltip). Long names are truncated; hover shows the full name. The pipeline name opens the menu to select, create, rename or delete; the gear opens options. On the right, before the commands, the work’s language pair appears in short, the same for all its pipelines. Pipeline operations are blocked while processing.
The red icon at the bottom of the window resets all translations and their audits, after a confirmation. It is off, with the reason, while the pipeline runs or when there is nothing to reset.
Next to each prompt title you see where its text comes from: Default, Custom or the name of the saved template in use.
steps: Open the configuration with the gear in the Studio's top row, or with Ctrl + comma. The title is the pipeline name; the tabs are General, Stages, Quality control, Memory, Glossary and Prompt preview.

In General choose the mode and edit the Translation context with the pencil: audience and register. Languages are not set here: they are the work’s Languages. Confirm with the checkmark or discard with X. It is never empty: it starts from a default text (English into Italian) that you can rewrite or replace with a saved template; the circular arrow restores it. Translation, refinement, audit and coherence receive it; languages are never added automatically to LLM prompts. The DeepL pair stays visible and is enabled only in DeepL mode. Unused stages are disabled; switching modes preserves their configuration.

In Stages and Quality control choose service, model and instructions for each stage. Once translations exist the model is closed by the lock: opening it leaves already translated chunks on the previous model. Explanations appear when you hover titles and rows.
In Memory set phrase memory and translation examples (DeepL mode does not use them); in Glossary assign the dictionary and save its terms with the disk icon.

Prompt preview shows each phase’s request piece by piece, each marked as fixed, yours, data or automatic with where it is changed; absent pieces stay disabled with the reason. Audit and Coherence show complete messages, DeepL the API request body. Expand text with the eye and copy it in full with the clipboard. Placeholders represent chunk data and optional context. The backend builds requests as for execution, without contacting services. Unused stages are disabled; audit and coherence remain available with DeepL.

Pipelines have no language pair of their own: in the DeepL stage choose the pair for standard translation. Automatic source detection is available, but a glossary requires an explicit source. DeepL Context is separate from the Translation context. Previews and logs show the API body; the configuration preview uses a chunk-text placeholder.

blocks.title: Testing and running
paragraphs: Use Test on a representative segment to inspect the result while keeping configuration editable. Then switch to production and choose whether to process one segment or several.
The estimate beside the controls applies to the selected action. It is approximate: usage depends on the submitted text and response. Statistics show available usage data after processing.

You can cancel execution. Completed results remain available; before resuming, check which segments will be processed. Rerunning unverified segments can replace their results. During execution you cannot switch pipelines or create a new one. Memory, Review and Document remember the selected subtab when you visit another tab.

To see the real request for a chunk, open it in the Studio and choose “Open chunk” in Prompt preview: the same pieces fill with its text, neighbouring chunks, checked memory phrases and previous translation; Audit and Coherence use the current translation and say so when there is none. If models, prompts, the Translation context or DeepL options change after an interruption, resuming tells you.

While a chunk is being translated, its translation text is covered by a gold veil reading “Translation in progress…” and cannot be edited: the result arrives when the stage finishes. The stage column in the margin stays usable; other chunks stay free.

In the Studio's Memory tab, References shows similar phrases already in memory, with where they come from; the circled check decides which to use in the translation. Memory opens once the translation is verified: saved pairs are removed with the bin, new ones are checked and added with the disk, which never deletes anything.

In Prompt preview, Structure mode, system prompts (roles, rules, headings, response format, user message) are locked: unlock them to edit like the other prompts, with System templates and reset. The lock closes when the window closes; the response format asks for an extra confirmation.
In the same view the switch of an optional piece turns it off for that phase only; a switched-off piece stays as a grey line, from which you turn it back on.

blocks.title: Reusing instructions
paragraphs: Save a prompt as a template to reuse it in other work: while editing, the bookmark asks for a name (Enter saves, Esc cancels) and the book opens the list of saved templates, with search; a click applies the one you pick. Templates are organised by context, such as stage instructions, assessment or the Translation context, and are deleted from the language resources.
The wand control rewrites the prompt through the configured service. Review the proposed text before using it: it is model-generated and may change your instructions.

features.title: Importing, editing and exporting
features.intro: The document view places source and translation side by side. Editor controls let you edit text, check formatting and compare stage outputs.

blocks.title: The translation studio
paragraphs: The main bar stays on the left: from there you move to another area, and the translation closes. While the pipeline is running its entries are off.

The top row leads back to the catalogue and shows the translation name, the open pipeline and the mode icon: click the work name to rename it, the pipeline name opens the menu to select, rename, create or delete one, the gear opens its options. On the right are the work’s language pair in short with the icon that opens “Languages of the work”, then import, export, the workspace language resources and delete.

The Tools column on the right starts with translate, Multiple chunks with the number of segments and the costs. Below are Glossary, Memory (similar phrases and extraction), Preview, Review (Audit, Notes, Source notes and History) and Document (Index, Statistics and Coherence). Collapsed, it keeps only the translate button visible.

blocks.title: Importing and dividing text
paragraphs: Use Import in the studio’s top row. Supported formats are TXT and Markdown up to 50 MiB, DOCX up to 100 MiB and PDF up to 50 MiB. DOCX extraction is experimental; PDFs must contain text rather than images alone.
Check the preview before confirming. Automatic segmentation divides text using a target word count. Markdown provides additional heading options.

The import window opens large. On the left are Work languages, Model and Chunk splitting; on the right the counts, the card or segment view (two small round icons) and the chunk preview at full height. At the bottom are the word check, Cancel and Import.

Work languages apply to all its pipelines. For each side, Source and Target, you can choose the Language (historical ones too, searchable by Italian name, English name or code), the Variety (only those of the chosen language, for example medieval Latin; disabled until you choose a language) and a free Note on period, area or hand. All are optional and the x clears a field. A new work starts with source not specified and target Italian; if the Library knows the book’s language, it is proposed as the source.

You can change them later from the Studio top row: click the languages icon on the right, next to the pair, edit, and press Confirm (nothing is saved otherwise). This is blocked while the pipeline runs. If phrases saved from this work have other languages, Glossa asks whether to update them: text and measures do not change and the previous version stays in the history.
Choose a size appropriate for the text and review segment boundaries. Text files using an encoding other than UTF-8 must be converted before import.

blocks.title: Editing and formatting
paragraphs: The editor menu provides writing, preview and split views, text size, copying and Markdown tools. Use the controls for bold, italic, headings, lists and footnotes.

Inspect and compare stage outputs to see where the text changed: the controls sit in a column in the right margin of the translation page, next to the scrollbar. At the top the stages in pipeline order, then comparison and the pairs to compare; the one you are viewing is highlighted. Enable source editing with the pencil only when you need to correct the original; its translation will be flagged for updating, with the ochre “Source changed” label next to the title.

When the translation is ready, mark it as verified with the check next to the “Candidate translation” title: it turns green, the text locks and automatic translation of unverified segments skips it. Marking it as verified also clears “needs updating”: it means you checked it against the current original. Return it to draft with the same control. When a control is off, hover it to read why.

Review → History lists the segment’s versions, newest first: who produced it (Pipeline or Manual), when, and which is current and which verified. A version is written at every pipeline pass, at every save with the disk if the text changed, and on verification. Restore puts the text back on the page and writes it as a new version, without deleting the others; it is off on a verified translation. Versions cannot be deleted and cannot be named yet.

Settings → Appearance sets theme, accent, interface font, document text (size, line height, reading layout) and highlights. Settings → Languages shows the language list in use and downloads it again from the official sources; retired languages stay readable.

blocks.title: Reading status indicators
paragraphs: Above the document a window of seven circles keeps the open segment still in the middle. Single arrows move to the neighbouring segment, double ones jump by seven; the wheel over the circles scrolls them, a click opens one. On the right are the open segment's stage indicators and the magnifier to search the whole document. The central mark shows whether a segment is ready, processing, completed or in error.

Corner indicators identify audit findings, notes, a verified translation (green) and a source changed after translation (ochre). The triangle marks the current segment. The tooltip provides a full summary.
Glossary and Document (Index, Statistics, Coherence) cover the whole document; Memory and Review the open segment. They all live in the Tools column.

You cannot leave the Studio while translation is running: wait until it finishes or stop processing. If saving fails, use “Retry”; technical details remain in the log. Disabled tabs stay reachable with Tab so you can read why they are unavailable, but cannot be opened.

blocks.title: Exporting
paragraphs: Open Export and choose TXT, Markdown, HTML, DOCX or bilingual Markdown. Segment separators apply only to TXT and Markdown.
Check incomplete segments: standard formats may use the source text where a translation is missing. Bilingual format shows the source, translation and any audit results.
Export does not necessarily recreate the imported document’s layout. Review the generated file, including footnotes and annotations, before delivery.

glossary.title: Dictionaries and glossary
glossary.intro: A dictionary contains terms and their required translations. Assign it to a project to use it as the pipeline glossary.

blocks.title: Preparing a dictionary
steps: Open Language Resources in the workspace and select Dictionaries.
Create a dictionary or choose an existing resource. The pencil beside the title edits it on the same row.

Use +: the new entry appears at the top with focus on its term. The pencil edits a pair; the notebook opens notes. The check finishes editing the entry; the disk saves the dictionary. You can also import CSV or TSV.
Assign the dictionary to the project and check its entries in the Tools column’s Glossary tab.

blocks.title: Sharing entries
paragraphs: Linking a dictionary to several workspaces keeps one shared resource. Create copy produces an independent dictionary instead.
A local override or exclusion applies only in the current workspace. Use this when a term needs different wording in another research context.

blocks.title: Checking terminology
paragraphs: The pipeline receives instructions to follow the glossary. Still check the result: a model may ignore or misapply an entry.
With highlighting on, the Glossary legend distinguishes source terms, matching translations and missing translations. Highlighting shows textual matches, not a check of meaning.
The glossary specifies required wording. Phrase memory instead suggests references to select for each segment.

blocks.title: Managing prompt templates
paragraphs: Each Prompt Template has a title and preview. The eye shows the full text; hover the icons for scope, workflow and model. Search names and text, and filter by Stages, Quality control, Translation context, System, Memory or OCR. If a saved template has a scope the app no longer recognises, it is left out of the list and a notice names it; the other templates stay available.

The + command opens the form; the pencil edits an existing template. Enter its name, scope, workflow and text; a default provider and model are optional. Label hints explain where the instructions will be used.
Choose a provider and model to Refine; unavailable commands explain missing credentials or fields. The disk saves and the cross cancels. Use a template’s trash command and confirm to delete it.

blocks.title: General resources and editing scope
paragraphs: In General language resources, the workspace filter shows all linked dictionaries, including shared ones. You always edit originals here; filtering only changes the list.

In an open dictionary the sharing icon identifies the shared original; the shield identifies local corrections. The hint explains where changes apply. Local corrections affect only the guest workspace; the adjacent plus explains that new entries are added to the shared original.

The disk and “Save and close” respect this scope. A save error keeps the window open; “Close without saving” discards edits. Rename and delete affect the shared original. Choose a destination workspace to create, import or copy from general resources.

memory.title: Phrase memory and examples
memory.intro: Phrase memory lets you reuse approved bilingual pairs. Finding a match does not mean it is automatically used or saved.

blocks.title: Using saved phrases
paragraphs: Open Memory → References for the chunk. Glossa filters only by the target language and compares texts with an embedding matching the workspace model, dimensions and input profile. Adjust the threshold with the slider or, one hundredth at a time, with − and +; then select relevant references.

Each reference shows similarity and origin (“this document”, “another work in the workspace” or “another workspace”), then the original in book type and the translation below, with the language code in the margin and, at the top, the language pair with its varieties; one line gives work and chunk, and the “i” icon shows workspace, book and model. Results from this document come first, then the workspace, then the rest. Selecting it controls inclusion in the next translation, without changing the collection. Pairs already saved in the chunk remain in the Memory subtab; they are not automatically inserted among search results.

The globe next to refresh extends the search to other workspaces and unassigned phrases; the choice is remembered per workspace and is no longer in workspace settings. The target language and embedding compatibility still apply. Viewing a phrase does not link it to this workspace.

blocks.title: Saving new phrases
steps: Review the segment’s translation and mark it as verified.
Open Memory → Memory. Saved pairs are read-only and each has its own trash command.
Extract new proposals or add a pair manually.
Edit new pairs and select those to keep.
Use the disk command to add selected pairs. Existing pairs remain saved; use their own trash command and confirm to remove them.

blocks.title: Using a style example
paragraphs: A style example contains an entire segment and its translation. It guides the pipeline, while phrase memory retrieves individual relevant pairs.
After marking a segment as verified, open Audit and use the control to add it as an example. Review or remove it in pipeline settings. You can keep up to five examples.

blocks.title: Browsing the collection
paragraphs: Open Linguistic resources → Memories. Filter by workspace, all or unassigned; search texts and tags, or select a tag. General resources start with all entries; workspace resources start with the current workspace.

Pairs show source and translation side by side, with languages, an origin title and tags. Each entry uses one muted background, including its expanded details. The details control opens full provenance, date, editable tags and measurements. Select a model there and use plus to add it or the circular arrow to recalculate it; other models remain. OpenAI calculation requires a key and incurs costs, described in the confirmation. Each available embedding has its own row; the calculation command shows a spinner while running.

The pencil edits both memory texts without changing the original translation. Editing only the translation preserves embeddings. Editing the source recalculates all available embeddings and archives the previous revision. If any calculation fails, no changes are saved.

Add manual tags separated by semicolons. After confirmation, the bin removes the memory text, revisions and embeddings. The dictionary command copies the pair into the selected dictionary. CSV export preserves text, tags, provenance and models for visible phrases only.

When creating a translation, you can select a Library book and version. Without this choice, the book is “Not specified”. It is not inferred from the imported filename and page numbers are not invented.
If you edit the archived source, provenance continues to describe the initial extraction and the “Archived source” row identifies the edit. The book text does not change.
Deleting a translation preserves archived texts, book and provenance. They appear as unassigned memory entries and indicate that the translation is no longer available.

audit.title: Reviewing a translation
audit.intro: The Audit tab contains the segment’s automated assessment. Use it to identify passages that need checking, always comparing the source and translation.

blocks.title: Checking and correcting
steps: Open Review → Audit after translation and read findings about terminology, accuracy, fluency, grammar and consistency.
Check each finding against the text. A passage link may not locate the exact phrase.
Edit the translation or rerun the stage that needs revision.
Use Re-evaluate to update the assessment without translating everything again.
Mark the translation as verified when you approve it.

blocks.title: Checking document consistency
paragraphs: After completing the segments, run the consistency check from Document → Coherence in the Tools column. It compares translated passages for terminology and style variations.
This check is separate from assessing accuracy against the source. A positive rating does not replace human review.

annotations.title: Annotations and notes
annotations.intro: Use annotations to keep decisions, questions and problems with the relevant segment.

blocks.title: Adding a note
paragraphs: Select a passage in the translation and choose Add annotation from the context menu. You can also add an unanchored note in the segment’s Notes tab.
Audit findings can be converted into annotations. Choose Comment, Doubt, Problem or Approved according to the note’s purpose.
Approved is a note type; it does not verify the translation. Use the check next to the page title to protect a translation from reprocessing.

blocks.title: Checking anchors
paragraphs: Anchored annotations appear as footnotes in the preview. If you edit the phrase they refer to, check that the anchor remains correct.
Notes about a Library work are separate from translation annotations.

blocks.title: Handling imported footnotes
paragraphs: Footnotes imported from Markdown or DOCX remain in the project but are not translated automatically. The pipeline receives the body text without footnote markers or contents.
To include them in the final translation, review their wording and insert them in the appropriate position. Check the exported file.

context.title: Context and costs
context.intro: When translating a segment, Glossa can also supply neighbouring passages, terminology and examples. These references help maintain continuity across the document.

blocks.title: Checking what is sent
paragraphs: In pipeline options, Prompt preview in “Open chunk” mode shows each phase’s message for the chunk open in the Studio. Read its instructions and text without calling the model or incurring charges.
Revision receives the source and draft. Formatting receives only translated text. Consistency review compares translated passages.

blocks.title: Understanding caching and usage
paragraphs: Some services can reuse repeated request content through a cache. Savings depend on the service, model and actual reuse; they are not guaranteed.
Anthropic caching is off by default. You can enable it in the pipeline and choose extended retention, considering how often you reuse the same instructions.
Statistics show tokens, cache usage and calculated costs when those data are available. A token is a unit of text used by the model, not necessarily a word. DeepL measures billed characters instead.

In the Tools column, under the commands, one line shows the next run estimate and what was spent on the open segment; a click opens the cost panel, with a per-stage table for each. Spent also counts model calls: a re-translated segment or a review loop adds calls, so they are not runs.

providers.title: Configuring providers
providers.intro: Configure services under Settings → Models, then choose a provider and model for each pipeline stage.

blocks.title: Remote services
paragraphs: Glossa integrates Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek for LLM stages. DeepL supplies the initial translation in DeepL Hybrid. Each service requires its own key and an account with API access.
Availability also depends on the model, quota and connection. Check a configuration on one segment before processing a long document.
Keys are kept in the system credential store when available, otherwise in an encrypted local store. Backups exclude them.

blocks.title: Custom endpoints
paragraphs: In Custom, create a profile with a name and base URL. Specify whether it requires a key and test the connection. Select that profile in the stage and enter the model name.
Remote addresses must use HTTPS. HTTP is accepted only for localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1. Available options depend on the compatible service you configure.

blocks.title: Parameters and unavailable controls
paragraphs: Temperature and reasoning depend on the model. A low temperature reduces variation but does not guarantee a correct translation. Some combinations do not allow it to be adjusted.
If a control is disabled, read its tooltip: a key or project requirement may be missing. Resolve that requirement before trying again.

ollama.title: Using Ollama
ollama.intro: Ollama runs models on your computer or a server you configure. To work without sending text to remote services, use a local server for all required operations.

blocks.title: Connecting the server
steps: Install Ollama and download a model compatible with your hardware.
Start the Ollama server if your installation does not start it automatically.
Open Settings → Models → Ollama and check the URL and connection status.
Refresh the model list, then select Ollama and the model for the required stages.
Try one segment and check speed, quality and memory usage.

blocks.title: Adjusting the model
paragraphs: Larger models require more memory and may take longer. If processing is too slow, shorten the segments or use a model your computer can run comfortably.
Use Think options only when the model supports them. Advanced options must be a valid JSON object; invalid values are not saved.
For structured assessment, Glossa sets Ollama’s temperature to zero. This does not guarantee identical or correct assessments.

shortcuts.title: Shortcuts and controls
shortcuts.intro: On macOS, use Cmd instead of Ctrl. Global shortcuts, except Ctrl + Enter and Ctrl + S in the Studios, do not apply while you are typing in an editable field.

blocks.title: Translation and project
paragraphs: Ctrl + Enter starts the selected translation action, including from a text field. Segment mode requires a selected segment.
Ctrl + S saves the open translation and modified language resources, even while typing on the pages. During automatic translation, saving the translation is deferred.
In the transcription Studio, Ctrl + S saves a version of the page to the history right away, even while typing on the page.
Ctrl + E opens export when the document has segments. Ctrl + comma opens pipeline configuration.

blocks.title: Navigation
paragraphs: Ctrl + 1 through Ctrl + 9 selects one of the first nine segments. Ctrl + H opens this guide section.
Tab moves focus between controls. Enter or Space activates them. Use arrow keys, Home and End in tab bars. Esc closes the open dialog or menu.
Hover over an icon control, or focus it with the keyboard, to read its description and any requirements.

troubleshooting.title: Solving a problem
troubleshooting.intro: Read the displayed message and identify the operation that failed. Change one setting at a time to check the cause.

blocks.title: Translation will not start
paragraphs: Check the selected provider’s credentials, model and connection. For Ollama, confirm that the server is running and the model is installed. For DeepL, also check quota and the remote glossary.
If the message concerns memory or processing time, try a shorter segment. For quality problems, compare stage outputs before changing both model and prompt.

blocks.title: A source or page will not open
paragraphs: Check that the source accepts the search type you used. No results and a source that failed to respond are different outcomes; inspect the monitor.
In the viewer, check local-only reading, the selected version and whether the repository drive is connected. Missing pages may require a library connection.

blocks.title: Work appears to have stopped
paragraphs: Open the job details. Waiting may indicate a temporary service limit; Paused requires resuming. An error instead shows its cause and any retry controls.
If saving fails, check the data directory and free disk space. Treat changes as unsaved until the status bar confirms completion.

blocks.title: Reading the program's messages
paragraphs: The bottom panel has three tabs: messages from the running translation, the system log, and jobs. The panel command in the status bar always opens it on the system log, which opens anywhere and shows what the program wrote while working: searches, downloads, storage, saves. New lines arrive by themselves while you watch.

Filters narrow by area and by level, and the search box works on the text of each line. Third-party library lines stay hidden until you ask for them: on their own they are most of the file. The data in curly braces is colored as in a code editor: the braces command turns the colors on and off. Clearing the view hides the current lines without touching the file on disk: new ones keep arriving, and reloading brings them all back.

blocks.title: Collecting information
paragraphs: When reporting a problem, include the version, operating system, action taken and message received. The status-bar console provides access to operations.
Request details may contain document text. Review them before sharing. The log directory is shown below.

overview.title: Getting started
overview.intro: Glossa lets you collect digital sources, read digitised works and translate documents with help from language models. This guide explains how to use the features available in the current version.

blocks.title: Starting a translation
steps: Open Settings → Models and configure the service you want to use. For Ollama, check that the server is running and a model is installed.
Create a workspace and a project within it. A workspace groups projects and resources used together.
Import a document and check its text and segment boundaries in the preview.
Set the languages and pipeline, then try translating one segment.
Review the result, process the remaining segments and export the document.

blocks.title: Finding your way around
paragraphs: The Dashboard shows work in progress with what is left, what to resume, items requiring attention, current jobs and this month's work. Its Search tab searches across multiple sources or within one source, including by identifier.

Statistics show how your work is going: forecasts, working days, spend, models, quality, OCR accuracy, glossaries. Choose the period and workspace at the top. Hover a card title to see what it measures. With too little data, a card says so instead of showing a number.
The Library contains works you have added to the catalogue. Translations lists projects from every workspace. Open a workspace to access its projects and resources.

The left bar holds the Dashboard, the areas in working order and the workspaces; at the bottom the general menu: save all, language resources, settings, help and language. Collapsed, the icons remain and a click opens the page without expanding it.

Library, Transcriptions and Translations each have their own ink: petrol, sepia and indigo. You see it in the area icon in the left sidebar, in the short rule under the large title and in a slightly different background paper. State colours do not change: green always marks what is selected or active.
Hover over an icon control, or focus it with the keyboard, to read what it does. Sidebars can be resized or collapsed.
Overview and Statistics cards can be moved: grab the handle to the left of the title and drag the card higher, lower or into the other column. The arrangement stays as you left it.

blocks.title: Data and available features
paragraphs: Working data is saved on your computer. When you use a remote service, the text needed for the operation is sent to that service. For local-only processing, also check the services selected for assessment, memory and prompt refinement.
Glossa is in private beta. Transcription, text recognition in scans and some advanced workflows remain incomplete. PDF text import is available, but it does not perform OCR.

projects.title: Workspaces and projects
projects.intro: A workspace organises projects and shared resources. Each translation project belongs to one workspace.

blocks.title: The Translations catalogue
paragraphs: The Translations page gathers the translations of every workspace and is laid out like the Transcriptions page: shelves on the right, search and quick filters above the list, three views (list, covers, table) at the end of the title row.

Each row shows the translation name in italics and, below it, the source and target languages. At the end of the row: workspace, translated segments out of the total, verified segments and the completion bar, green when every segment is verified. A translation with no imported text says so instead of the counts.

The shelves are All, Recent (edited in the last 30 days), Not started (no segment translated), In progress and Verified (every segment verified). Quick filters narrow by workspace and language pair; the workspace filter stays when you leave the page and come back. You can sort by name, last edit or progress, and group by workspace or language pair.

Clicking a row opens the translation in the editor. Hovering a row shows its commands: rename (the name becomes a field: Enter saves, Esc cancels) and delete. In the cover and table views the same commands sit in the three-dot menu.

blocks.title: Creating and identifying a project
paragraphs: Create a translation with the «+» next to the Translations title, or from the workspace page. The window asks for the name, the workspace (unless it already knows it) and, optionally, the file to translate, in the same formats as the editor import. The file is read as soon as you choose it: if it cannot be read, for example a scanned PDF with no text or a file not in UTF-8, the reason appears under the field and nothing is created. The chosen book shows its title in its row; the book icon opens a searchable list (title, with the copy below) and the x removes it. Pressing Create opens the translation in the editor with the import preview, where you choose Work languages and segments; if you close the preview the translation stays empty and you can import the file later from the editor. The workspace name, description and icon are edited in its settings.
A project can contain multiple pipelines with separate settings and results. Select the pipeline you want to work on before changing its configuration.

blocks.title: Saving your work
paragraphs: A translation saves itself shortly after the last edit, as a whole: source text and every segment. The status bar, bottom right, shows its state: saved, unsaved changes, saving or error; hover it to read the time of the last save and, after an error, the reason.

To save right away use the disk at the top of the translation page (on the source page when only the source is open), or Ctrl + S even while typing on the pages; use Cmd on macOS. Besides saving, the disk writes a version to the history of every segment changed since its last version; automatic saving writes none. The disk stays off when there is nothing to save and no new version to write and while automatic translation runs, because the pipeline saves by itself at the end. If a save fails, the disk turns red and retries it.

Going back to the catalogue, or elsewhere from the main bar or the path at the top, saves the translation before closing it. If that save fails you stay in the translation with the error in view, instead of losing the last edit.

blocks.title: Sharing and moving
paragraphs: Works and dictionaries can be linked to several workspaces without creating copies. Local terminology overrides apply only in the workspace where you make them.

Moving a translation leaves its text unchanged and moves its extracted phrases with it. It then uses the new workspace’s resources. Earlier operation costs remain attributed to the original workspace.

blocks.title: Archiving or deleting
paragraphs: Archive a workspace to retain it outside the active list. Before deletion, you can choose to archive it, transfer its contents or remove them.
Deleting a project removes its translation data. Works and dictionaries linked to a workspace remain in the general catalogue. Backups cover all workspaces and are not a way to transfer just one.

search.title: Searching for sources
search.intro: From the Dashboard open Search: a single field to look for works in the libraries or to open one whose identifier you know. Results enter the Library only when you decide.

blocks.title: Searching
steps: Open Search from the left bar, under Dashboard.
To the left of the field choose where to search: all libraries, a single one, or a custom choice made in the advanced criteria.

Type the words and start with the command next to them. To narrow down, open the advanced criteria, first tab of the right column: title, author, printer, material, years. Aggregators such as Europeana are added on purpose; Europeana needs a key in the Library settings.

Results appear as sources answer. Above the list choose the order: by relevance, year, author, or title. When the data needed to judge a criterion is missing, the result stays in the list marked “incomplete data”.

The searched words are in bold and in the accent color where they appear, in the row and in the opened record data. An icon next to the row marks results whose words are not in the record: on Gallica, found only in the page text. "Exact phrase", in the advanced criteria, searches the words in sequence where the library supports it. Library of Congress and National Library of Scotland are not part of "all": choose them by hand in the advanced criteria.
When more results are available, the command at the bottom of the list asks every source that has them. The command spins while they arrive, then the new results appear at the bottom.
The new search command clears words and criteria, keeping the sources you chose.

blocks.title: Reading the results
paragraphs: Each row shows author, year, place, and printer, then the title; in small print library, pages, and “PDF available” when there is one. Open the row for every detail.

Libraries that search by field — Gallica today — receive title, author, printer, material and years exactly as you write them, and answer only with works that match. The others receive the words; the criteria then drop results that state something else. Next to each criterion, the hint tells which of the chosen sources really search it.
The same work arriving from several libraries is a single row, with the number of copies. Open the row to choose which copy to use.
A record can exist without a readable reproduction: the row then says “not viewable”. A network error does not mean the work is missing.

blocks.title: Opening an identifier or an address
paragraphs: Type or paste the identifier of a work, or its address, in the same field. If a library recognises it, an “Open on …” row appears above the results: press the command next to it and the work opens, ready to add to the Library.
A full address also opens with Enter. An IIIF manifest from an institution not listed opens the same way, by pasting its address.

When the list stays empty, or you are looking at one source only, a command opens the library’s own search in the browser with the same words. What Glossa queries is what the library offers to a program, rarely its whole catalogue: when in doubt, search on their site, copy the address of the work and paste it here.

blocks.title: Sources, history and saving
paragraphs: The Sources tab, on the right, has one row per library: state, how many results arrived, “retry” after an error, and the filter to look at that source only.
The search history lives in the next tab: from there you reopen an earlier search with its criteria and results.

Add to Library saves the record. Add to workspace also links it to the chosen workspace. The same manifest is not duplicated. Extend to aggregators starts a linked search using only newly selected aggregators.
You can switch screens while the search goes on. Closing Glossa stops it; history remains available when you reopen it.

sources.title: Using the Library
sources.intro: The Library is the catalogue of works you have kept. Use it to organise them, inspect their metadata and read their images.

blocks.title: Finding a catalogue entry
paragraphs: Every work looks the same in search, in the Library, and in the Studio: author, year, place, and printer stand out, then the title, cut after two lines. Hover over the title to read it in full.

On the right are the shelves: All, Recent (added or opened in the last 30 days), To download, Being transcribed, Not linked to a workspace, Archived. Below are your collections and the saved views. To create one, press the "+" next to the heading, type the name and press Enter; Esc cancels.

Above the list, on its own line, you search every piece of data about the work — title, author, printer, place, notes, identifier — and below it you narrow down with the quick filters: type, century, language, library, download, workspace. Each value shows how many works it has. Sort by title, author, year, recently added or recently opened.

Next to the Library title choose how to see the list: rows, covers or table. The table has a column for author, title, year, place and printer, library, pages and state; click the author, title or year header to sort. With “Group” you split the list by century, author, library or collection.
A saved view remembers the chosen filters: turn on at least one filter, then press the "+" of the saved views and give it a name. The view updates by itself as you add works.
Link works to workspaces and collections to organise them. A work can have several links without duplicating its record or files.

The item page shows every field it knows about, including those the library did not fill in: they stay empty and you write them with the pencil, as you already do for title and author. The library's original value is kept and can be restored. The essential fields are always in view, the rest sit in groups that open and stay as you leave them.

blocks.title: Working on several works at once
paragraphs: Hold Ctrl (⌘ on the Mac) and click several works to choose them; with Shift you choose every work between the last choice and the one you click. You can also press the check mark that appears on the left of the row. A click without keys opens the work.

A command bar for the choice appears above the list: put the works in a collection (a new one too), link them to a workspace, download them, archive them or bring them back to the catalogue. Esc or the cross clears the choice; changing shelf or collection clears it by itself.
To put works in a collection you can also drag them onto the collection in the shelves column: the dragged row moves, or the whole choice if the row is part of it.

The commands of a single row appear when you hover over it. At the bottom left you link the work to a workspace or add it to a collection; at the top right, in three groups, are the transcription, the image commands (download, verify, reduce, free space) and those to archive or delete. In the covers and the table the same commands sit in a menu. The small line also tells how far the work has gone: being transcribed, transcribed, translated.

blocks.title: Reading and editing the record
paragraphs: Open a work. The panel beside the viewer contains Work, Digitisations, Organisation and Notes. Notes about the work are saved automatically.

You can correct the title, author, date and language. Each override is separate from the original and can be removed. Resynchronise with the library retrieves fresh data and clears manual overrides while retaining notes and images.

blocks.title: Reading pages
paragraphs: Use thumbnails, arrows or the page-number field to navigate. Zoom enlarges the image, and Glossa remembers your reading position.
Local file identifies a page in the repository; Online file identifies a page read without a permanent copy. The tooltip shows its source and actual dimensions.
Enable local-only reading to prevent the viewer from requesting images from the library. Missing pages display a notice. The option resets when you close the work.

blocks.title: Downloading and saving
paragraphs: In Digitisations, choose a resolution and start downloading the work. A different resolution creates another local version. You can choose which version to open.
Save page keeps only the displayed image at the dimensions shown in the tooltip. It does not request a new image at the configured resolution.

blocks.title: The PDF of the work
paragraphs: Some libraries, besides page-by-page images, offer the same work as a PDF. In search results the row says “PDF available” when there is one. Opening the row shows the full status — available, not available, or not verified when the library did not answer — with the declared pages and the pixel size of the first page, the only hint about scan quality before downloading.

In the work record the PDF is a row of the book section, below the image copies: there it states whether it is available, whether it has been downloaded, how much space it takes and how many pages it has. The check command queries the library again, for when the PDF was published later; the same check runs on resynchronisation.

From the same row you choose what to display: the PDF or the images. The viewer always states which of the two is on screen, because the pages of the PDF and those of the image sequence do not correspond. A very large PDF does not open in the built-in viewer: open it with the system application.
Every check has a deadline: if the library is busy or does not answer, the status stays “not verified” and you can try again. No wait is left hanging and no request blocks the others.

blocks.title: Archiving, freeing space or deleting
paragraphs: Archive hides the work from the active list and keeps its files. The subsequent offer to free space is optional.
Free space removes downloaded pages while keeping the record. Deleting a local version removes only that version. Deleting the work removes its record, links and files without a recycle bin.
Before deleting files, finish or cancel jobs that use them. Pausing is not enough.

storage.title: Downloads and storage
storage.intro: Downloads, integrity checks and image reduction run as background jobs. Follow their progress from the status bar.

blocks.title: Managing jobs
paragraphs: Open the jobs panel at the bottom right. Each entry shows progress and status; expand it for details, attempts and errors.
Pause requests a stop at the next checkpoint; Resume continues from there. Cancel ends the job and keeps files already saved. After a failure, you can start another attempt.
Waiting may indicate a library rate limit. A countdown refers to the next attempt, not the end of the download. Paused means the job needs to be resumed.
Jobs stop when the app closes. On reopening they remain paused, unless automatic download recovery is enabled under Settings → Jobs.

While reading you can act on a single page: keep it, take it at the highest resolution — it replaces the one you have — bring it back to the book size, or remove it from the computer. A removed page stays excluded and does not come back with a new download, until you ask for it again.

A work keeps one copy only, with one file per page: asking for the book at another size replaces the one you have, and recompression rewrites the pages lighter without changing their dimensions — there is no way back without downloading again.

blocks.title: Reviewing and deleting past jobs
paragraphs: The bottom panel shows running, waiting and recently finished jobs: it is the view of what is happening now. The bin command in its header takes the finished rows out of the view, so new jobs read clearly; it deletes nothing.

The full list lives in the right-hand column of the Overview, and can be narrowed, widened or closed with the command at the top left of the column. Every row expands like in the bottom panel, with phase, attempts, times and error.

At the top of the column there is a free-text search and two rows of commands: the first picks how the job went (running, succeeded, failed, interrupted), the second the kind of work. Several choices can be on at once.

The bin at the top of the column deletes the finished jobs the filters are showing: with the filters off that is all of them, with a filter on only those. No job is ever deleted automatically. Search jobs are the exception — they stay as long as the search they belong to, otherwise its history would lose pieces.

blocks.title: Choosing a resolution
paragraphs: Under Settings → Library → Images, choose page and thumbnail dimensions. A setting made for an individual work overrides the general value.
The size specifies the desired long edge. Depending on the service and request mode, the received image may be larger or smaller. Maximum resolution requests all available detail.

Existing downloads are unchanged. To obtain a smaller version without downloading again, use image reduction: it creates a new copy and retains the original. Delete a version only after checking the result.

blocks.title: Data directory and file repository
paragraphs: Settings → Data → Folders separates the data directory, containing projects and catalogue data, from the image repository. The repository can be on an external drive.

Changing the data directory copies the database and requires a restart to use the new location. Changing the repository does not move existing downloads: choose an empty directory or an existing Glossa repository.
Keep the database on a local drive. If you synchronise the repository, configure the service to retain files on your computer; online placeholders are not enough.

blocks.title: Checking files and clearing the cache
paragraphs: A quick check verifies that files exist. A full check also inspects their contents. Results distinguish intact, missing, corrupt and unassociated files.
Verification does not automatically delete or download files. Cleaning up files without an associated work requires a separate command.
The cache temporarily retains images and search responses. Clear it in storage settings without deleting downloaded repository pages. To keep a work permanently, download it.

blocks.title: Adjusting library requests
paragraphs: Under Settings → Library, assign a network profile and image request mode to each library. Profiles control concurrency, request rate, retries and waiting periods.
Profile changes require an explicit save. Higher limits do not guarantee faster downloads: the service may slow or reject requests.

backup.title: Backup and restore
backup.intro: A backup keeps data from all workspaces in one file. It excludes repository images, exported documents and service credentials.

blocks.title: Creating a backup
paragraphs: The file holds work records, annotations, transcriptions, translations with their history, glossaries and phrase memory, searches with the results they returned, the operations log, services configured by hand, and the list of exported documents.
steps: Open Settings → Data → Backup & Restore.
Choose password protection to encrypt the contents, or Glossa-only format, which is not encrypted.
Choose where to save the file and wait for confirmation.
For a password-protected backup, also keep the recovery code shown after saving somewhere outside the application.

blocks.title: Restoring a backup
paragraphs: Pause active searches, select the backup file and enter its password or recovery code if required. Glossa checks that the backup is valid and compatible before asking for confirmation.
Restoring replaces data in all existing workspaces. It does not merge collections or import one workspace. Create another backup first if you need to retain the current state.
If both the password and recovery code are lost, encrypted backup contents cannot be recovered.

blocks.title: Recovering images and connections
paragraphs: Files already in the repository remain on disk. After restoration, Glossa checks them and may offer to download missing files at their recorded resolutions.
Recovery depends on the libraries remaining available. Keep separate copies of images and exported documents you need to preserve. On a new installation, also re-enter service keys.
